newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore exports seen down 3.4 pct in September.
newsitem.headline: Singapore exports seen down 3.4 pct in September.

text.p: Singapore's exports are continuing to suffer as result of a worldwide slowdown in electronics and computer industries, financial institutions polled by Reuters said on Thursday.

Twelve economists produced an average forecast of a fall of 3.4 percent year-on-year in nominal terms in the city-state's non-oil domestic exports. This compares with a fall of 6.3 percent in August and a rise of 6.3 percent in July.
Forecasts for September ranged from a fall of seven percent to a rise of five percent year-on-year.
"The export figures for September, and for the next few months, are going to be bad," said Desmond Supple, senior emerging markets economist at Independent Economic Analysis (IDEA) in Singapore.
"We are seeing very, very nascent signs of a recovery in the key electronics sector, but it will take a while to filter through to the Singapore economy," he added.
Electronics and related products account for about half the city-state's industrial production and almost 60 percent of its non-oil exports.
Worldwide demand for electronics and computer parts fell sharply early this year due to an overhang of inventory, mainly in the United States.

Recent U.S. figures suggest the electronics slump is now easing. The U.S. Semiconductor Industry Association said on October 8 that the key North American "book-to-bill ratio" rose in September to 0.99 from 0.93 in August. A figure under 1.00 means new orders are lagging existing deliveries.
But economists stress there is usually about a six-month time lag between a turnaround in electronics consumer markets and a real rise in demand for suppliers.
"The recovery is coming," said Liew Yin Sze, economist at Singapore brokerage J.M. Sassoon. "One has only to look at the semi-conductor industry in the U.S. and Japan to see that."
"But it is too optimistic to see that translating into stronger exports in 1996...It should pick up at the start of 1997," he said.
Maminder Singh, economist at Nomura Securities, said he was fairly opimistic of a quick recovery in Singapore exports.

"We see August as the bottom for the electronics industry," he said. "People are already saying orders have begun to pick up. The rebound may not be strong yet, but even if it doesn't come immediately, it should begin to come in the fourth quarter of the year."
The same poll produced an average forecast of a 1.5 percent year-on-year rise in Singapore's consumer price index (CPI) of inflation. The CPI rose 1.4 percent year-on-year in August.
The government is expected to publish its official figures for exports and CPI for September in the next few days.
